title: How Rodney Dangerfield Worked, Live From LA
summary: Live recording at the LA Podcast Festival in which Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile comedian Rodney Dangerfield (born Jacob Cohen): his neglected childhood, early joke writing, the Jack Benny-derived stage name, his Ed Sullivan and Carson breakthrough, the Dangerfield's comedy club, films such as Caddyshack, Easy Money and Back to School, Miller Lite ads, his lawsuit against Star magazine, his final Howard Stern interview and death, and his rejection by the Academy. The episode includes an ad break for a podcast (The Message) and a listener-facing close with social media contact info.
topics: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences rejection

entities.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

segments.title: Live show opening and banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck greet the live audience at the LA Podcast Festival, banter about merchandise and sponsors, and tease the Rodney Dangerfield topic.

segments.title: Dangerfield's no-respect persona and inner pain
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Dangerfield's no-respect stage persona, his depression and heaviness, and the sad contrast seen in his 1980s TV interviews.

segments.title: Childhood neglect and early life
segments.summary: Dangerfield was born Jacob Cohen to a vaudevillian father who left and a mother who neglected him. He raised himself from about age eight, worked delivering groceries, and describes being molested for money as a child.

segments.title: Joke writing and early career
segments.summary: Dangerfield began selling jokes at about fifteen or sixteen, kept thousands of handwritten jokes in a bag, and worked at a Catskills resort and as a singing waiter and diver before marrying Joyce Indig and moving to New Jersey.

segments.title: Comeback, name change and Jack Benny character
segments.summary: After quitting comedy at 27, Dangerfield returned at about 41 with a persona. He legally changed his name to Jack Roy and took the name Rodney Dangerfield from a Jack Benny character after a club owner suggested it.

segments.title: Ed Sullivan, Carson and national fame
segments.summary: A dress-rehearsal spot got Dangerfield noticed by Ed Sullivan, leading to many late-night appearances, including a record number on Carson. Carson had earlier blackballed him over a joke accusation before they reconciled.

segments.title: Opening Dangerfield's club in New York
segments.summary: Dangerfield borrowed about a million dollars to open his own New York comedy club so he could stay home with his children. The club succeeded, repaid its loan quickly, and became known for its HBO specials and launching comics such as Seinfeld, Chris Rock and Jim Carrey.

segments.title: Film career: Kubrick, Caddyshack, Easy Money
segments.summary: Dangerfield appeared in Kubrick's The Killing and The Projectionist, then became a hit in Caddyshack, where he disliked the filming process. He later wrote and starred in Easy Money, which Roger Ebert praised.

segments.title: Podcast sponsor break
segments.summary: The hosts promote The Message, an eight-part podcast from Panoply and the podcast theater about cryptologists decoding a message from space.

segments.title: Back to School, Miller Lite, and later career
segments.summary: Back to School was a major hit in 1986. Dangerfield's 1980s Miller Lite commercials, a Grammy for the No Respect album, Smithsonian display of his shirt and tie, the rap single Rappin' Rodney, Simpsons appearance, Broadway show and a romance novel are covered.

segments.title: Lawsuit, Howard Stern interview, and death
segments.summary: Dangerfield sued Star magazine for libel and was awarded modest damages. In his final Howard Stern interview he discussed his childhood before undergoing surgery, falling into a coma, having a heart attack and dying. His funeral attendees included Jim Carrey and Michael Bolton.

segments.title: Academy rejection and website
segments.summary: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences initially rejected Dangerfield's membership, and he built a website. The Academy later relented but he declined. The hosts close the content by joking about the cover-comedian idea.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: The hosts thank the LA Podcast Festival, mention social media and email contacts, and say goodbye.
